question: Can an arbitrarily capable but computable learning pipeline be trapped by a very large dataset into selecting a simple model that fails badly on fresh data, even when the globally best model is much more complex?

key_findings.claim: The formal target is the whole computable learning pipeline, not merely a hypothesis class or optimizer.
key_findings.evidence: The procedure P may include sampling, training, validation, regularization, hyperparameter selection, and pseudorandom computation. A deceiver is an available dataset for which P returns a locally optimal model whose prediction error on a fresh extension is at least delta relative to the optimum on the total dataset.

anchors.section: Definitions of deceiver and unpredictable deceiver

key_findings.claim: For every computable learner, arbitrarily large available datasets can make its selected optimum exceptionally simple while concealing a much more complex global optimum.
key_findings.evidence: Lemma 3.1 invokes Busy Beaver growth to construct available data of size at least BB(n) whose selected model has complexity bounded by a computable function of n. Lemma 3.2 then appends fresh data so the globally optimal model can have arbitrarily larger Kolmogorov complexity and differ by the requested prediction-error margin.

key_findings.claim: The main theorem makes the bad global model uncomputable from the learner, error threshold, and locally selected model.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 3.1 states that sufficiently large total data admit a low-complexity apparent optimum on the available portion while the fresh-data error is at least delta. The dataset-size condition grows with BB of total-data complexity after accounting for the learner and delta, and the globally optimal model is an unpredictable deceiver rather than merely a difficult finite search target.

key_findings.claim: Under the paper's universal-distribution setup, unpredictable deceivers receive a notable asymptotic probability comparison, but this is not evidence that ordinary empirical datasets commonly exhibit the pathology.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 3.2 compares the algorithmic probability of an unpredictable deceiver with that of any particular sufficiently large dataset, up to a multiplicative constant depending on P. The result is conditional on a universal-style distribution and nonconstructive size thresholds, so reading it as an observed prevalence estimate would overstate the theorem.

key_findings.claim: Complexity caging is proposed as a research direction, not proved as a remedy.
key_findings.evidence: The discussion suggests constraining total-data complexity relative to the learner, controlling selected-model complexity as data complexity grows, and stating a universal-style data distribution. The authors explicitly leave open whether these conditions can rule out all deceivers.

method.core_idea: Use algorithmic information theory and uncomputability to construct data extensions on which simplicity-seeking behavior becomes a trap for every fixed computable learning system.
method.mechanism: Encode the learner and data as programs, use Kolmogorov complexity to compare locally and globally optimal models, use Busy Beaver growth to force an enormous simple-looking prefix, and use halting-probability arguments to make the required global optimum unrecoverable from the learner's available information.
assumptions: The end-to-end learning system is computable; any randomness inside it is pseudorandom or otherwise part of a computable procedure.
Datasets, models, prediction errors, and optimization choices admit finite program encodings.
Kolmogorov complexity is measured relative to a fixed universal description language, with invariance constants absorbed asymptotically.
The probability claim uses an algorithmic universal distribution rather than a domain-specific empirical data distribution.
Dataset sizes may be nonconstructively and astronomically large because the bounds involve Busy Beaver functions.

techniques.role: Formalizes the simplicity of datasets and selected models independently of a particular parametric class.
Creates available-data prefixes whose required size outruns every computable scale.
Makes the globally optimal extension impossible to recover from the learner and its local output.
Separates apparent fit on available data from performance on a carefully constructed fresh continuation.
Places the construction within a universal-distribution probability argument.

evaluations.metric: Existence of a delta-deceiver with bounded local-model complexity
evaluations.result: Theorem 3.1 gives a sufficiently large dataset whose locally selected model is simple and whose fresh-data error is at least delta
evaluations.baseline: Globally optimal model on the full dataset

evaluations.metric: Algorithmic probability up to a P-dependent multiplicative constant
evaluations.result: Theorem 3.2 lower-compares an unpredictable deceiver with any particular dataset beyond the stated size condition
evaluations.baseline: Probability of an arbitrary fixed sufficiently large dataset

evaluations.metric: Kolmogorov complexity of P's selected model
evaluations.result: Lemma 3.1 bounds model complexity by a computable function despite a prefix size at least BB(n)
evaluations.baseline: Unbounded complexity of a later full-data optimum
No real dataset, learner, or computable diagnostic is supplied

limitations: Kolmogorov complexity, Busy Beaver values, and the relevant halting probability are uncomputable, so the proof does not produce a practical detector.
The size thresholds are nonconstructive and can be vastly beyond any realistic dataset.
The result is a worst-case existence construction, not an empirical estimate of how often simplicity bubbles occur in ordinary machine learning.
The formal treatment centers on prediction or regression; broader classification claims are discussed rather than developed comparably.
Truly noncomputable stochastic sources fall outside the fixed computable-pipeline premise.
The proposed complexity-caging conditions are hypotheses without a theorem showing that they prevent deceivers.
failure_modes: A reader treats an algorithmic universal prior as the natural distribution of a specific scientific or industrial domain.
The existential construction is advertised as a finite counterexample that can actually be generated or recognized.
Complexity upper bounds are approximated with a compressor and then mistaken for the theorem's uncomputable quantities.
Fresh data are chosen adaptively by an adversary, while a claimed application assumes iid sampling from a fixed distribution.
The conclusion 'more data hurts' is substituted for the narrower statement that a carefully extended dataset can invalidate a simple local optimum.
Complexity caging excludes useful complex generators or is imposed without testing whether it removes the targeted pathology.
reusable_insights: Model the complete data-selection and tuning pipeline when making universal claims about learning behavior.
Separate worst-case existence, probability under a formal prior, and prevalence under a real data distribution.
Audit simplicity principles against extensions of the observed dataset, not only interpolation within it.
Treat uncomputability theorems as boundary results that motivate operational proxies rather than as ready-made diagnostics.
State the complexity of the data generator relative to the learner whenever an Occam-style guarantee is proposed.
open_questions: Can a computable finite-sample proxy identify approaching simplicity bubbles with useful precision and recall?
Which realistic distributional assumptions convert the adversarial existence result into a quantitative risk bound?
Can complexity-caging conditions be proved sufficient, or is another deceiver construction possible inside the cage?
How does the result change for genuinely randomized algorithms and interactive human-in-the-loop learners?
Can analogous statements be made for classification, representation learning, or reinforcement learning without reducing them to scalar prediction?
What empirically measurable gap best distinguishes ordinary misspecification from the paper's formal unpredictable deceiver?

competitive_landscape.title: The Pitfalls of Simplicity Bias in Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Shah et al. show that neural networks can prefer simple predictive features and consequently fail under distribution shift or adversarial perturbations. The reviewed paper proves a learner-universal, uncomputability-based worst-case construction rather than studying a particular architecture on finite benchmarks.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Computability of Solomonoff Induction and Knowledge-Seeking
competitive_landscape.difference: Leike and Hutter classify computability properties of Solomonoff-style induction and knowledge-seeking agents. The reviewed paper uses related algorithmic-information limits to construct deceptive datasets for arbitrary computable learning pipelines.

competitive_landscape.title: The no-free-lunch theorems of supervised learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Sterkenburg and Grünwald argue that standard no-free-lunch results depend on a purely data-driven framing and that model-relative inductive biases can be justified. The reviewed theorem instead fixes any computable pipeline, including its bias, and constructs a sufficiently large extension that defeats it.

competitive_landscape.title: No Free Lunch versus Occam's Razor in Supervised Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Lattimore and Hutter reconcile Occam-style induction with no-free-lunch by using universal priors and structured problems. The reviewed paper identifies a complementary boundary: even simplicity-favoring computable learners admit unpredictable deceivers at sufficiently extreme scales.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Every fully automated computable learning system admits sufficiently large datasets that induce an unpredictable simplicity bubble, with a universal-distribution probability comparison for such deceivers.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Two construction lemmas and Theorems 3.1-3.2 combine Kolmogorov complexity, Busy Beaver growth, and halting-probability uncomputability at the level of an end-to-end learner.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The distinctive contribution is the formal learner-wide impossibility construction and its framing of apparent simplicity as a trap. Its practical force is conceptual: it does not establish prevalence, provide a computable test, or show that the proposed cage works.

reviewer_notes: Read all 19 extracted pages, including definitions, both construction lemmas, main theorems, discussion, and complexity-caging proposal. Four primary arXiv records were checked on 2026-08-23. Logical structure and claim scope were passage-checked; the algorithmic-information proofs were not independently rederived line by line.
